passages.original: « Omnes, i inquit, i sub peccato nascimur, quorum ipse ortus in vitio est » (Ambrosius, de Pœntientia, lib. 1, cap. 2 vel 3), Quid ad ista respondes? ilIa de Ambrosio dixit praeclara Pelagius; ista pro me contra te manifesta pronuntiavit Ambrosius : istum reprehende de quo dicit magister tuus, quod eum ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere; et qui sanos judices quæris, istum nega sanum, ut te plane profitearis insanum. Sed indignaris homo piissimus, quod parvuli non renati, si moriantur ante propriae voluntatis arbitrium, propter aliena dicantur peccata damnari, ab eo qui commendat charitatem suam in nobis, qui dilexit nos, ct Filio suo non pepercit , sed pro nobis illum tradidit : quasi non de illo gravius conquerantur stulti ct indocti similes tui, qui dicunt, Utquid creat, quos impios futuros et damnandos esse præscivit?
passages.english: "We are all," he says, "born under sin, we whose very origin is in fault" (Ambrose, On Penance, book 1, chapter 2 or 3). What do you answer to this? Pelagius said those splendid things about Ambrose; Ambrose pronounced these plain things for me against you. Find fault with this man, of whom your master says that not even an enemy dared to find fault with him; and you who seek sound judges, deny that this man is sound, so that you may openly declare yourself unsound. But you, a most pious man, are indignant that unreborn little ones, if they die before [having] the choice of their own will, are said to be condemned on account of the sins of another, by him who commends his love toward us, who loved us and did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us: as if foolish and unlearned people like you did not complain more gravely about him, saying, Why does he create those whom he foreknew would be ungodly and to be condemned?

passages.english: But I will show you my own, whom you accuse all the more wickedly the more cunningly [you do it]. For in this case, where the question of original sin is at issue, on account of which you judge me, under the name of the Manichaeans, deserving of the most savage insults, Cyprian is mine, who, though he said that a little one had committed no sin, yet did not keep silent that it had contracted from Adam, by its first birth, the contagion of sin (Letter 64, to Fidus). Hilary is mine, who, when expounding what is read in the Psalm, My soul shall live and shall praise you, says: "He does not reckon that he lives in this life; for he had said, Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me (Ps. 50:7). He knows that he was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin" (On Psalm 118:175). Therefore Paul's flesh was a body of death" (On Penance, book 1, chapter 2). passages.original: Hanc ergo fidem antiquitus traditam dico atque fundatam : tu renuis, et cui relucteris, non respicis. Numquid huic eam a diabolo dicere poteris inspiratam? Numquid iste Manichaeus est? numquid Marcion, Faustus, Adimantus? Non utique" sed longe his dissitnilis, longeque contrarius. Pelagius certe dicat quis iste sit. Ille, Hic est, cujus fidem, et puris- simum in Scripturis sensum ne inimicus quidem ausas est reprehendere. Quid est, Juliane? ubi te vides! Ille, cujus ne inimicus quidem reprehendere ausus est fidem, hanc habebat fidem, quam tu ita reprehendis, ut eam trihnas conciliis malignantium. Ecce non est eorum, sed cst Ambrosii: quia vera est, quia sana est, quia, ut dixi, antiquitus tradita atque fundata est, hæc et mea est. Non ego hanc in Italiam (quod vos gemere dicilis) eructavi: sed potius ab isto episcopo Italiae hanc praedicante et docente 1 lavacrum regenerationis accepi.
passages.english: This faith, then, I say was handed down and established from of old: you reject it, and you do not consider whom you are resisting. Will you be able to say that it was inspired in this man by the devil? Is he a Manichaean? Is he Marcion, Faustus, Adimantus? Certainly not, but far unlike them, and far opposed [to them]. Let Pelagius at any rate say who this man is. He [says]: "This is he whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures not even an enemy dared to find fault with." What is this, Julian? See where you are! He whose faith not even an enemy dared to find fault with held this faith, which you find fault with so much that you assign it to councils of malicious men. See, it is not theirs, but it is Ambrose's; because it is true, because it is sound, because, as I said, it was handed down and established from of old, it is mine too. I did not belch this out into Italy (as you say you groan); rather, I received the washing of regeneration from this very bishop of Italy as he preached and taught it.
passages.notes: "trihnas" read as "tribuas"; "dicilis" as "dicitis"; "ausas" as "ausus". The stray "1" before "lavacrum" is a footnote mark.

Ilinc 8 loquens beatus Ambrosius: « Caro, » inquit, « in naturam regressa vigoris sui, agnoscit altricem; atque ausu deposito contumaciæ, moderationis9 animæ conjugatur arbitrio: qualis fuit, cum inhabitanda paradisi secreta suscepit, antequam veneno pestiferi serpentis iurecta sacrilegam famem sciret, divinorumque memo- riam præceptorum animae sensibus inhaerentem edacitatis studio praeteriret. passages.english: And therefore, although both were already evil, yet the will led the desire, not the desire the will: it did not precede the will, nor resist the will. Finally, if the will had been turned away from the unlawful deed before the sin was completed, the unlawful desire would have been calmed without any effort. Speaking of this, blessed Ambrose says: "The flesh, returned to the nature of its own vigour, recognises its nurse; and, laying aside the boldness of defiance, is joined to the judgement of the soul's moderation: such as it was when it received the secret places of paradise to dwell in, before, infected by the poison of the deadly serpent, it knew a sacrilegious hunger, and in its eagerness for eating passed over the memory of the divine commands that clung to the soul's senses. From here sin is reported to have flowed, as from the body and the soul as parents: while the nature of the body is tempted, the soul, being unsound, suffers with it;
passages.notes: "iurecta" read as "infecta"; "mate sana" read as "male sana". Ambrose's text here is somewhat obscure.

passages.original: Utinam catholicos agnosceres sacerdotes, qui longe priusquam esse coepistis, dixerunt concupiseentiam carnis, quae concupiscit adversus spiritum, quamvis adversus eam etiam spiritus concup!scat, quæ lex intelligitur esse peccati, resistens legi mentis post peccatum quod in paradiso perpetratum est, humanam vitiasse naturam : unde sine illa modo nascitur nemo; eique spiritus adversatur in sanctis, ut justc vivant, pugnando contra illam, donec perfecta hominis salute, et carne cum spiritu plenissime concordante jam non sit. Dicit Ambrosius , per praevaricationem primi hominis in naturam vertisse dissensionem carnis et spIritus; eamque dissensionem sic I Cyprianus ostendit, in quo Poeno Punicam dialexim, ut puto, irridere non audes, quod facere in me ausus es : « Est, » inquit, « inter carbem et spiritum colluctatio, et discordantibus adversum se invicem quotidiana congressio, ut non qua volumus ipsa faciamus, dum spiritus coelestia et ditina quærit, caro terrena et saecularia concupiscit: et ideo petimus inter duo ista, ope et auxilio Dei concordiam fieri, ut dum et in spiritu et in carne voluntas Dei geritur, quae per eum renata est anima servetur. Quod aperte atque manifeste Apostolus sua voce declarat: Caro, inquit, concupiscit adversus spiritum , et spiritus adversus carnem: hœc enim invicem adversantur sibi ; ut non ea quœ vultis, ipsa faciatis » ( De Oratione Dominica). Hanc tu concordiam carnis et spiritus , quam noa optare, et a Domino dicit oraro Cyprianus, nec in paradiso ante peccatum fuisse concedis : aut si fuit, cur non fateris eam per praevaricationem primi hominis vitiata periisse natura3, beataeque paci animae et corporis miseram successisse discordiam ?
passages.english: Would that you recognised the catholic bishops, who, long before you began to exist, said that the concupiscence of the flesh, which lusts against the spirit (although the spirit also lusts against it), which is understood to be the law of sin resisting the law of the mind, has vitiated human nature since the sin committed in paradise: hence no one is now born without it; and the spirit opposes it in the saints, so that they may live justly by fighting against it, until, when man's salvation is perfected and the flesh is in fullest harmony with the spirit, it no longer exists. Ambrose says that the dissension of flesh and spirit turned into nature through the transgression of the first man; and Cyprian shows that dissension thus, in whom, a Carthaginian, you do not dare, I think, to mock the Punic speech, as you dared to do with me: "There is," he says, "a struggle between flesh and spirit, and a daily encounter between those at odds with one another, so that we do not do the very things we wish, since the spirit seeks heavenly and divine things, the flesh desires earthly and worldly things; and therefore we ask that, by God's help and aid, harmony may come about between these two, so that, while God's will is carried out both in the spirit and in the flesh, the soul reborn through him may be preserved. This the Apostle declares openly and plainly in his own words: The flesh, he says, lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do the very things you wish" (On the Lord's Prayer). This harmony of flesh and spirit, which Cyprian says we desire and pray for from the Lord, you do not grant existed even in paradise before sin; or if it did, why do you not admit that it perished when nature was vitiated by the transgression of the first man, and that a wretched discord succeeded the blessed peace of soul and body?
passages.notes: "Punicam dialexim": Julian had mocked Augustine as a 'Punic' disputant.

passages.original: AUG. Quid calumniaris, quid falso criminaris, nec quos et quales Ecclesire doctores crimineris attendis? Non cujusquam Manichæi, sed sancti Ambrosii verbis tibi respondeo : « Deus quos dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit i (Lib. 7, in Luc. IX, 58). Hoc in veritate facit, hoc in veritate Scripturarum divinarum Intellexit Ambrosius : sed judicium, cum alios facit, et alios non facit, occultum est. Propter quod dicitur homini per hominem, sed non ab homine : 0 homo, tu quis ea, qui respondeas Deo ? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit, Quid me fecisti sic ?
passages.english: AUG. Why do you slander, why do you accuse falsely, and not consider whom, and what sort of teachers of the Church, you are accusing? I answer you not in the words of some Manichaean, but in those of saint Ambrose: "God calls those whom he deigns to, and makes religious whom he wills" (Book 7 on Luke 9:58). This he does in truth; this Ambrose understood in the truth of the divine Scriptures: but the judgement, when he makes some [so] and does not make others, is hidden. For this reason it is said to man through a man, but not by a man: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me thus?

He therefore calls those whom he deigns [to call], and makes religious whom he wills (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke 9:58), he who made the man whom he willed, one [man], without any preceding merits of human will, the mediator of God and men.

passages.original: IV. JUL. Quodque ait in Epicurum Tullius, manifesto argumento nun dici ilia subtiliter, quod cujuscemodi homines passiln sibi ea profitentur placere. Id isti, sicut omnia, more perverso s, ad sapientiae putant testimonium pertinere.
passages.english: IV. JULIAN. And what Tullius says against Epicurus, that it is clear proof that those things are not said subtly, that men of every sort everywhere profess that they approve of them. This these people, as with everything, in their perverse way, think pertains to the testimony of wisdom.

passages.original: Quanto magis ergo multa sunt, eis additis quæ habent alii plura , alii pauciora? a quibus tamen omnibus liberat ista gratia, de qua dictum est, Ex multis delictis in justificationem (Rom. v, 16). « Fuit enim Adam, et in illo fuimus omnes; periit Adam, et in illo omnes perierunt. » Ambrosius hoc dixit (Lib. 7 in Luc. xv, 24) : calumniose, non erat Manichæus. Parvulos contagium mortis antiquæ prima nativitate contrahere, Cyprianus dixit (Epist. 64, ad Fidum) : calumniose, non erat Manichaeus.
passages.english: How much more, then, are they many, when those are added which some have in greater number, others in fewer? Yet from all of them this grace sets free, of which it was said, From many offences unto justification (Rom. 5:16). "For Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished." Ambrose said this (Book 7 on Luke 15:24): slanderously [you say it], he was not a Manichaean. That little children contract the contagion of the ancient death by their first birth, Cyprian said (Letter 64, to Fidus): slanderously [you say it], he was not a Manichaean.
passages.notes: 'calumniose' is elliptical and ironic; it seems to mean that any charge of Manichaeism here would be slander.

Illum aspice qai dixit, Per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum : sicut enim in Adam omnes moriuntur, sic et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur ( I Cor. xv, it, 22) : Apostolus Christi est, non discipulus Manichæ. Illum aspice qui dixit, < Omnes homines sub peccato nascimur »(Ambrosius, de Pœnitentia, lib.1, cap. 2 vel 3 ) : episcopus est catholicus, non Manichæus, aut Pelagius, aut Pelagianus haereticus. Quapropter quoniam peccatum operis punit et homo, peccatum autem originis nonnisi Deus : ideo Deus, cum se dicat peccata patrum reddere in filios, praecipit tamen homini ne pro peccatis patrum damnet et filios.
passages.english: and stop begrudging Christ the physician the healing of little children, lest the wrath of God remain upon them, who says, I will render the sins of the fathers upon the sons. Look at him who said this: he is God, not a Manichaean. Look at him who said, Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive (1 Cor. 15:21, 22): he is an Apostle of Christ, not a disciple of Manes. Look at him who said, "All we human beings are born under sin" (Ambrose, On Repentance, Book 1, ch. 2 or 3): he is a catholic bishop, not a Manichaean, or Pelagius, or a Pelagian heretic. Therefore, since man too punishes the sin of deed, but only God [punishes] the sin of origin, God, though he says he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons, nevertheless commands man not to condemn the sons also for the sins of the fathers.

passages.original: AUG. Dic quod dicturus es, egregie corrector; quo auctore deceptor est credendus Ambrosius , de quo ait Pelagius magister tuus, quod ejus fidem, et purissimum in Scripturis sensum ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere (u). Tu eum reprehende ; fortior enim es atque potentior inimicus crucis Christi, quam si esses inimicus Ambrosii ;
passages.english: AUG. Say what you are going to say, distinguished corrector: on what authority is Ambrose to be believed a deceiver, of whom your master Pelagius says that not even an enemy dared to find fault with his faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures? You find fault with him; for you are a stronger and mightier enemy of the cross of Christ than if you were an enemy of Ambrose;
passages.notes: "deceptor" in the text read as "deceptor" (deceiver).

passages.original: Sed ne arroganter, vel fallaciter vobis dicere videantur nostram esse catholicam, ille eam proferat, cujus fidem et purissimum in Scripturis sensum, sicut eum prædicat vester ipse Pelagius, ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere (a). Dicit ergo Ambrosius, hanc discordiam carnis et spiritus, per prævaricationem primi hominis accidisse nostræ naturæ (Lib. 7 in Luc. xu) : vos aulem dicitis, ex vi consuetudinis : Manich;ci dicunt, ex commixtione duarum naturarum coæternarum, boni scilicet et mali.
passages.english: But lest [our people] seem to you to say arrogantly or deceitfully that ours is the catholic [view], let him bring it forward whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures, as your own Pelagius proclaims of him, not even an enemy dared to criticise. Ambrose, then, says that this discord of flesh and spirit befell our nature through the transgression of the first man (Book 7 on Luke 12); but you say [it comes] from the force of habit; the Manichaeans say [it comes] from the mixture of two co-eternal natures, namely of good and evil.
passages.notes: The subject of 'videantur' is unexpressed; likely 'we' or 'our people'.

passages.original: Auc. Hanc ego concupiscentiam carnis malum dico esse, quam dicit Joannes a Patre non esse, et quam dicit Ambrosius in naturam nostram ex primi hominis prævaricatione vertisse (Lib. 7 in Luc. XII) ; unde Joannes volens homines intelligi, eam dicit ex mundo esse. Hanc concupiscentiam carnis et Manichcus malum dicit;
passages.english: Augustine: This concupiscence of the flesh I call evil, which John says is not from the Father, and which Ambrose says turned into our nature from the transgression of the first man (Book 7 on Luke, 12); hence John, wishing men to be understood, says that it is from the world. This concupiscence of the flesh the Manichaean too calls evil;
passages.notes: "Manichcus" read as "Manichaeus". "volens homines intelligi" is obscure; rendered literally.

passages.original: XLIII. JUL. Sequitur ergo ut verecundiam deponas, ac manente amicitia cum magistro, Cynicis faedereris : quos tamen aliquorum, ut Cicero in Officiis refert, etiam Stoicorum argumenta comitantur. « Arguunt quippe communem honestatem, quod ea quæ re turpia non sint, verbo flagitiosa ducamus : illa autem quae re turpia sint, nominibus appellemus suis. Latrocinium perpetrare, fraudem facere, adulterium committere, re turpe est, sed dicitur non obscene : liberis operam dare, honestum est re, nomine obscenum. Pluraque in eam sententiam, ab eisdem, » inquit, contra verecundiam disputantur.
passages.english: XLIII. JULIAN. It follows, then, that you should lay aside modesty and, keeping your friendship with your master, ally yourself with the Cynics; whom, however, as Cicero reports in On Duties, the arguments of some, even of Stoics, accompany. "For they find fault with common decency, because we regard as shameful in word things that are not base in fact, while things that are base in fact we call by their own names. To commit robbery, to practise fraud, to commit adultery is base in fact, but is spoken of without obscenity; to apply oneself to begetting children is decent in fact, obscene in name. And many more things to this effect," he says, "are argued by these same people against modesty."
passages.notes: 'faedereris' read as 'foedereris'.

passages.original: Numquid posses in carnis concupiscentia vel libidine bestias hominibus comparare, nisi etiam illos primos parentes generis humani tanquam corruptibilia gerentes corpora, etiamsi non peccassent, crederes fuisse morituros? Ac hoc in hæresis vestrae errore % novitio sic catholica damnat Ecclesia, ut Pelagius princeps vester id sibi inter caetera objectum apud quatuordecim episcopos orientales, a quibus judicibus audiebatur, damnationis suae timore damnaret (a). In que judicio profecto etiam tu ipse damnatus es, qui dicis Adam ita factum, ut sive peccaret, sive non peccaret, moriturus esset : contradicens Apostolo dicenti, Corpus mortuum eat propter peccatum (Rom.
passages.english: Could you compare beasts with human beings in the concupiscence or lust of the flesh, unless you also believed that those first parents of the human race, as bearing corruptible bodies, would have died even if they had not sinned? And the Catholic Church so condemns this in the novel error of your heresy that Pelagius your chief, when this was raised against him among other things before fourteen Eastern bishops, by whom as judges he was being heard, condemned it out of fear of his own condemnation. In that judgment you yourself too were certainly condemned, who say that Adam was so made that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die: contradicting the Apostle, who says, "The body is dead because of sin" (Rom.
passages.notes: "eat" read as "est"; stray "%" omitted.

passages.original: An ideo te arbitraris effugere insequentes plagas auctoritatis atque rationis, quia in societate libidinis, ad currum tui erroris, homines et asinos jungis? Non de pecoribus, sed de hominibus loquebatur Ambrosius, ubi ait: « Servatum est igitur, ut ex viro et muliere, id est, per illam corporum commixtionem, nemo videatur expers esse delicti » (In Isaiam). Itane iste, iste doctor Ecclesiae I accusator erat sanctorum, et patronus asinorum ?
passages.english: Or do you think you escape the pursuing blows of authority and reason because, in the fellowship of lust, you yoke men and asses to the chariot of your error? Ambrose was speaking not of beasts but of men when he says: "It was therefore preserved that, from man and woman, that is, through that mingling of bodies, no one should be seen to be free of fault" (On Isaiah). Was this man, this teacher of the Church, then an accuser of the saints and a patron of asses?
passages.notes: Stray 'I' after 'Ecclesiae' omitted as a footnote mark.

passages.original: Itane non accusat susceptam tuam, qui dicit concupiscentiam carnis adversus spiritum ex prævaricatione primi hominis in nostram vertisse naturam (Ambrosius, lib. 7 in Luc. XII) ? Et quis est hic? iMe scilicet, cujus fidem et purissimum in Scripturis sensum, sicut eum Pelagius auctor tuus pradicat (Pelagius, de Libero Arbilrio, lib. 3; apud Augustinum, de Gratia Christi, nil. 46, 47), ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere. Adversus hunc accusatorem tuam defende susceptam.
passages.english: Does he not, then, accuse your protégée, who says that the concupiscence of the flesh against the spirit turned into our nature from the transgression of the first man (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 12)? And who is he? That man, of course, whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures, as your authority Pelagius proclaims him (Pelagius, On Free Will, book 3; in Augustine, On the Grace of Christ, nos. 46, 47), not even an enemy dared to find fault with. Defend your protégée against this accuser of hers.
passages.notes: "susceptam" (feminine) refers to concupiscence/lust, which Julian has 'taken up' to defend; "accusatorem tuam" read as "suam".

passages.original: Auc. lnstitutionem laudavi corporum, quae bona est etiam in malo homine, non malum, sine quo nascitur nemo : quod til nolens cum Ambrosio dicere unde sit, adjuvas Manichæum dicentem quod ex aliena natura sit.
passages.english: AUGUSTINE. I praised the formation of bodies, which is good even in a bad man, not the evil without which no one is born; and you, being unwilling to say with Ambrose where this [evil] comes from, help the Manichaean who says that it comes from an alien nature.
passages.notes: 'til' read as 'tu'.

passages.original: Verum liis ut res postulabat impletis, juvat te vel mediocriter convenire, qua fiducia tu, cum Hieronymi scripta collaudes, dicas in Christo HOD fuisse peccatum, cum ille in Dialogo illo, quem sub nomine Attici et CriLoboli, mira et ut talem fidem decebat venustate composuit, etiam quinti Evange- Iii (a), quod a se translatum dicit, testimonio nitatur ostendere, Christum non solum naturale, verum etiam voluntarium habuisse peccatum, propter quod se cognoverit Joannis baptismate diluendum. De alio etiam testimonio Joannis evangelistæ, flagitium ei assuit falsitatis (b). De quo opere tu in illa epistola, quan Alexandriam destinasti, ita gloriaris, ut dicas Pelagium, Scripturarum ab eo oppressum molibus, arbitrium liberum vindicare non posse. Verum illi operi a catholico viro, qui pulsatus fucrat, obviatum est. Nunc vero ad boc commemorationem ejus tantummodo feci, ut te recognosceres non solum Scripturis sanctis, sed nec ipsis tui dogmatis adjutoribus consonare.
passages.english: But these things having been completed as the matter required, I am pleased to put to you, even if only modestly, [the question] with what confidence you, while praising the writings of Jerome, say that there was no sin in Christ, when he, in that Dialogue which he composed under the names of Atticus and Critobulus with a remarkable elegance befitting such faith, tries to show even by the testimony of a fifth Gospel, which he says he translated, that Christ had not only natural but also voluntary sin, on account of which he knew he must be washed by John's baptism. Concerning another testimony of John the Evangelist too, he stitched on him the shameful charge of falsehood. Of this work you boast, in that letter which you sent to Alexandria, so much as to say that Pelagius, overwhelmed by him with masses of Scripture, cannot defend free will. But that work was answered by a catholic man who had been attacked. Now, however, I have mentioned it only so that you might recognise that you agree not only not with the holy Scriptures, but not even with the very supporters of your own dogma.
passages.notes: "HOD" read as "non". The "fifth Gospel" is presumably the Gospel according to the Hebrews. The passage on John's testimony is obscure: "ei" may refer to Christ (charged with falsehood over John 7:8).

passages.original: 14,15), qua Christum dicit non aliter expertem delicti esse potuisse, nisi expers fuisset illius conceptionis, qaam commixtio viri et mulieris operatur. Ubi cernis esse consequens, ut si ego propter hanc sententiam sum Manichaeus, sit et Ambrosius : quia vero ille non est, neminem faciat vel , ostendat. ista sententia Manichæum. Hoc cum videas (non enim tale cst ut non possis hoc videre, vel possis hoc non videre), tantum tamen causæ bonitatedesel'eris, ut calumnieris milii nonaine Manichæi, nen imprudente ignorantia, sed pudente fallacia 1.
passages.english: 14:15), in which he says that Christ could not have been free of sin otherwise than by being free of that conception which the intermingling of man and woman brings about. Here you see that it follows that, if I am a Manichaean because of this statement, Ambrose is one too; but since he is not, this statement neither makes nor shows anyone to be a Manichaean. Though you see this (for it is not such that you cannot see it, or can fail to see it), you are nevertheless so abandoned by the goodness of your cause that you slander me with the name of Manichaean, not through imprudent ignorance, but through a shameless deceit.
passages.notes: 'pudente fallacia' is printed; 'impudente' (shameless) is the expected sense in contrast with 'imprudente'; translated accordingly. 'desel'eris' read as 'desereris'. 'vel , ostendat' read as 'vel ostendat'.

passages.original: Nos itaque imitamur eum, cum peccatum non facimus, non peccati concupiscentiam non habendo, sed non ei consentiendo : quamvis ita imitemur illum Sanctum sanctorum, cum bene vivimus, ut tamen non desit unde dicamus in oratione nostra, Dimitle nobis debita nostra ( Mattli. vi, 12 ). Ego autem non sic laudavi Hieronymum, quomodo Pelagius laudavit Ambrosium, quod ejus fidem et purissimum in Scripturis sensum ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere (De gratia Christi, nn. 46, 47). Ac per boc si quid mihi displicet, reprehendo in amici scriptis 1, sicut in meis.
passages.english: We therefore imitate him when we do not commit sin, not by not having the concupiscence of sin, but by not consenting to it; although we imitate that Holy of holies, when we live well, in such a way that there is still not lacking reason for us to say in our prayer, "Forgive us our debts" (Matt. 6:12). But I did not praise Jerome in the way Pelagius praised Ambrose, that not even an enemy dared to find fault with his faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures (On the Grace of Christ, nos. 46, 47). And for this reason, if anything displeases me, I find fault with it in a friend's writings, as in my own.

passages.original: Non hoc crat Apostolus, qui dixit : Corpus quidem mortuum est pro-pier peccatum (Rom. VIII, 10).Non hoc erat flilarius, qui dixit: « Ex peccato omnis caro est, a peccato scilicet Adam parentis1 deducta. » Non hoc erat Ambrosius, qui dixit: « Omnes sub peccato nascimur, quorum ipse ortus in vitio est. (De Pænitentia , cap. I vel 3). Utinam tu potius istorum Christi piscatorum retibus tcnaciter salubriterque capiaris : tunc accusativum casum, quo ipse a te ipso es accusatus, et ablativum, quo de Ecclesia catholica es ablatus, correctus melius declinabis.
passages.english: The Apostle was not this, who said: The body indeed is dead because of sin (Rom. 8:10). Hilary was not this, who said: "All flesh is from sin, that is, drawn down from the sin of Adam our parent." Ambrose was not this, who said: "We are all born under sin, we whose very origin is in fault" (On Penance, ch. 1 or 3). Would that you might rather be caught, firmly and to your salvation, in the nets of these fishermen of Christ: then, corrected, you will decline better both the accusative case, by which you have been accused by yourself, and the ablative, by which you have been taken away from the Catholic Church.
passages.notes: Wordplay: accusativus/accusatus and ablativus/ablatus cannot be fully rendered. 'flilarius' read as 'Hilarius'.

passages.original: AUG. Per unum hominem , in quo omnes peccaverunt, in mundum intrasse peccatum , dixit Apostolus, intellexit Ambrosius : sed eadem verba apostolica in suum perversum sensum conatur pervertere Julianus. Cur ei non ipse potius respondet Ambrosius? Audi ergo, Juliane : Omnes, inquit, in Adam moriuntur; quia ( per unum hominenl peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors ;
passages.english: AUG. That through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, the Apostle said and Ambrose understood; but Julian tries to twist these same apostolic words into his own perverse sense. Why does not Ambrose himself rather answer him? Listen then, Julian: "All," he says, "die in Adam, because 'through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death;

passages.original: Dico , inquit, plane propter delictum illos esse sub diabolo : ideo autem expertes non esse delicti, quia de illa commixtione sunt nati, quæ sine pudenda libidine non potest etiam quod honestum eat operari. Dixit hoc eliam beatissimæ memoriae Ambrosius ( Supra , de Nuptiis et Concupiscentia, lib. 2 , n. 15 ). 0 calamitosam hominis pravitatem ! o intentionem nefandam ! o falsitatem erubescendam !
passages.english: "I say," he says, "plainly that they are under the devil because of sin; but that they are not free of sin because they were born of that intermingling which cannot accomplish even what is honourable without shameful lust. Ambrose of most blessed memory also said this" (above, On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, n. 15). O the calamitous depravity of a man! O wicked purpose! O shameful falsehood!
passages.notes: The final exclamations are Julian's, quoted by Augustine.

passages.original: An, quoniam non invenis qua exeas, iram quidem simulas, non tamen iratus, sed turbatus exclamas? Verum in ipsis exclamationibus tuis audio, 0 Calamitosam hominis pravitatem ! Quia videlicet homo sum calamitosus et pravus, qui consentire cligo Ambrosio : essem vero beatus et rectus , si eligerem consentire Juliano. Audio, 0 intentionem nefandam ! Intentio quippe nostra nefanda est, quia opponimus Ambrosium Juliano : esset autem fanda, si Julianum praeponeremus Ambrosio.
passages.english: Or, since you find no way out, do you feign anger, and cry out, not angry but flustered? Yet in these very exclamations of yours I hear: O the calamitous depravity of a man! Because, of course, I am a calamitous and depraved man, who choose to agree with Ambrose; but I would be blessed and upright if I chose to agree with Julian. I hear: O wicked purpose! Our purpose is indeed unspeakable, because we set Ambrose against Julian; but it would be speakable if we put Julian before Ambrose.
passages.notes: Pun on 'nefanda' (wicked, lit. 'unspeakable') and 'fanda' ('speakable').

passages.original: Tam vero aperta est ista sententia , ut non aculus qui hanc intellexerit, sed anperfluus videri possit qui exponendam putaverit. Denique ut quod dico possit attendi, verba ipsa beatissimi catholici antistitis et hic ponam. Ait ergo ille, ille cujus3 fidem et purissimum in Scripturis sensum, Pelagius vester dicit, ne inimicum quidem ausum fuisse reprehendere ( Pelagius, de Libero Arbitrio, lib. 3); cum de nativitate Domini loqueretur : Ideo et quasi homo per universa tentatus est, et in similitudine hominum cuncta sustinuit : aed quasi de Spiritu natus abstinuit a peccato.
passages.english: Indeed this statement is so plain that whoever has understood it would seem not sharp, but whoever has thought it needed explaining would seem superfluous. Finally, so that what I say can be attended to, I will set down here too the very words of the most blessed catholic bishop. He says, then, he whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures your Pelagius says not even an enemy dared to find fault with (Pelagius, On Free Will, book 3), when speaking of the Lord's birth: "Therefore also, as a man, he was tempted in all things, and in the likeness of men he endured all things; but as born of the Spirit he abstained from sin."
passages.notes: "aculus" read as "acutus"; "anperfluus" as "superfluus"; "aed" as "sed".

passages.original: AUG. Valde contra Manichaeum est quod dixit Ambrosius. Nam Manichaeus alienam mali naturam nobis dicit esse commixtam; Ambrosius autem prævaricatione primi hominis nostram dicit esse vitiatam : in hac vero sententia de qua nunc agimus, nativitatem carnis Christi a caeterorum peccati carne discernens defendit Ambrosius, quam negat penitus Manichaeus. Quod ergo credit Ambrosius, hoc et ego : quod autem Manichæus, nec ille, nec ego.
passages.english: AUG. What Ambrose said is strongly against the Manichaean. For the Manichaean says that an alien nature of evil is mixed into us, whereas Ambrose says that our own [nature] was vitiated by the transgression of the first man. And in this statement which we are now discussing, Ambrose upholds the birth of Christ's flesh, distinguishing it from the flesh of sin of everyone else, which [birth] the Manichaean entirely denies. What Ambrose believes, then, I believe too; but what the Manichaean [believes], neither he nor I.

passages.original: Auc. IIic jam incipis confiteri, bane a nobis non esse confictam velut Ambrosii, sed vere esse sententiam I; quandoquidem sic te ab illo libcrarc conaris, ut dicas, « Numquid lcgi Dei aut operi Dei disputatorum scripta præjudicant? » Sed perge, dic caetera quibus impudentior inimicus fidei catholica: judiceris.
passages.english: AUG. Here you now begin to admit that this statement was not fabricated by us as if it were Ambrose's, but is truly his; since you try to free yourself from him by saying: "Surely the writings of disputants do not prejudge the law of God or the work of God?" But go on, say the rest, by which you may be judged a more shameless enemy of the Catholic faith.

passages.original: Nam si vera ratione defenduntur haec dicta, procul dubio veraciter defenduntur, et vera sunt: et si hoc ita est, recte asseritur originale peccatum, et dogma interimitur vestrum. Si autem falsa ratione defenduntur haec dicta, clara tua illa et benigna ratio non est ratio, sed deceptio. At enim « conjugia crebro laudavit • Ambrosius: hocet nos facimus. « Nullam, i inquis, cin corporibus affectionem a diabolo ille putavit insertam : » si affectionem bonam, nec nos; si malam, sicut ille, ita et nos. « Nec regno, « inquis, « diaboli divina opera, hoc est naturae membra, ille subjecit: » quasi adulterorum membra non sint divina opera et membra natune, quae tamen vitio, et per hoc diabolo constat esse subjecta.
passages.english: For if these sayings are defended by true reasoning, without doubt they are truthfully defended, and are true; and if this is so, original sin is rightly asserted, and your doctrine is destroyed. But if these sayings are defended by false reasoning, that clear and kindly reasoning of yours is not reasoning but deception. "But Ambrose often praised marriage": so do we. "He thought," you say, "that no affection in bodies was implanted by the devil": if a good affection, neither do we; if a bad one, as he [did], so do we. "Nor did he," you say, "subject the divine works, that is, the members of nature, to the kingdom of the devil": as if the members of adulterers were not divine works and members of nature, which nevertheless are evidently subjected to vice, and through this to the devil.

passages.original: AuG. Tibi quidem hoc videtur: sed verum non esse ( quod tu non vides) vidit Ambrosius , qui dixit expertes non esse delicti ex viro et muliere, id est, per illam commixtionem corporum natos (In Isaiam): nec tamen ipsam commixtionem cum ipsius naturae . institutione condemnat. Commixtio quippe conjugum procreandi causa, bonum est nuptiarum : sed ita fiunt nonnulla opera bona non sine malo vitiorum, sicut opera mala non sine bono membrorum.
passages.english: AUG. So it seems to you; but that it is not true (which you do not see) Ambrose saw, who said that those born of man and woman, that is, through that intermingling of bodies, are not free of sin (On Isaiah); and yet he does not condemn the intermingling itself along with the constitution of nature itself. For the intermingling of spouses for the sake of procreation is the good of marriage; but some good works are done not without the evil of vices, just as evil works [are done] not without the good of the members.

passages.original: Quid est ergo quod tam male sentis de illis sacerdotibus, quorum non, ut mentiris, deluis dicta, sed polluis, ut cis quasi dubitantibus velis persnadare, unde nec illus, nec nos dubitare convincis? Dona cst commixtio conjugalis, quæ fit causa procreandi. Sed Ambrosius, qui dixit ex commixtione utriusque sexus neminem esse cxpertem delicti , non commixtionem redarguit conjugalem; sed vidit malum, cujus bono usu fil illud, quod nemo catholicus dubitat esse opus bonum. Inania loqueris, superfluis tempus impendis : quod agitur deseris, et unde non dubitatur, tanquam dubitetur, vel cHam negetur, docere moliris.
passages.english: Why then do you think so badly of those bishops, whose sayings you do not, as you falsely claim, wipe away, but defile, so that you want to persuade them, as though they were in doubt, of that about which you prove neither them nor us to be in doubt? Conjugal intermingling, which takes place for the sake of procreation, is good. But Ambrose, who said that no one is free of sin from the intermingling of both sexes, did not censure conjugal intermingling; rather he saw the evil by whose good use that is done which no Catholic doubts to be a good work. You speak empty things, you spend time on superfluities: you abandon what is at issue, and you labour to teach what is not doubted as though it were doubted, or even denied.
passages.notes: 'deluis' read as 'deluis' (from deluo, wash away) contrasted with 'polluis'; sense somewhat uncertain. 'Dona' read as 'Bona'; 'cHam' as 'etiam'.

passages.original: Cur ergo eorum, quos prudentes viros dicis et catholicos sacerdotes, te dicta defendere atque deluere siue ullo pudore mentiris, si et ipsa dissiliunt fulminus tuis ? Si autem defenduntur atque deluunlur, et ob hoc manent integra, ipsis tu potius fulminaris. Nam quod ait Ambrosius, ex commixtione sexus utriusque conceptum expertem neminem esse delicti, aut falsum est, aut verum. Si falsum esse dicis; oppugnas ergo prudentium virorum et catholicorum, sicut tu fateris, sacerdotum dicta, non defendis ac deluis.
passages.english: Why then do you lie without any shame, saying that you defend and clear the sayings of those whom you call prudent men and catholic priests, if they too burst apart under your thunderbolts? But if they are defended and cleared, and for this reason remain intact, it is rather you who are struck by them. For what Ambrose says, that no one conceived from the union of both sexes is free of sin, is either false or true. If you say it is false, then you are attacking the sayings of prudent men and, as you yourself admit, catholic priests, not defending and clearing them.
passages.notes: "deluere" (to wash clean, clear) renders Julian's phrase; "fulminus" read as "fulminibus".

passages.original: AUG. Et nos pro modulo nostro populos aedificanius, hortando, obsecrando, arguendo, quod fecit Ambrosius; et tamen de originali peccato hoc seniimus et didimus, quod sensit et dixit Ambrosius, nec solus sed cum aliis magnis consortibus suis. Quos « antistitcs Ecclesiarum » cum « viros sani capitis » dicas; tu quali capite ista, quae illi notissima consensione didicerunt atque docuerunt, reprehcndis atrociter, defendisque fallaciter;
passages.english: AUG. We too, according to our small measure, build up the people by exhorting, entreating, rebuking, as Ambrose did; and yet concerning original sin we hold and have said what Ambrose held and said, and not he alone but with other great colleagues of his. Since you call them "bishops of the churches" and "men of sound head," with what sort of head do you fiercely censure, and deceitfully defend, those things which they learned and taught with a most well-known consensus?
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (aedificamus, sentimus, dicimus, antistites, reprehendis).

passages.original: per hoc cos sub potestate diaboli constitueret : tunc ergo te doclorc Manichæus esse desisteret. 0 quid perdidit, qui te audire non potuit ! Proindc quia propter hunc sensum Manichæum me esse dicis, profecto in hoe sensu perseverans , Manichæus, te auctore, Ambrosius hac excessit e vita. Non ergo illum defendere , quod nullo modo potes, sed dolere debes, quia docere jam non potes : quod si facere potuisses , magisterio tuo ille correptus atque correctus prohiberet utique in Ecclesia quam regebat, exorcizari etexsufflari baptizandos parvulos;
passages.english: …and thereby place them under the power of the devil: then, with you as teacher, he would cease to be a Manichaean. O what he lost, who could not hear you! Therefore, since you call me a Manichaean on account of this view, then certainly, by your verdict, Ambrose departed this life a Manichaean, persevering in this view. So you ought not to defend him, which you can in no way do, but to grieve that you can no longer teach him: for if you had been able to do so, he, reproved and corrected by your instruction, would surely have forbidden in the Church which he governed that infants to be baptized be exorcised and breathed upon;
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence; the subject of "constitueret" is unclear from the passage.

passages.original: nec commixtionem conjugum, vel opus diaboli, vel necessitatem diceret esse peccati: improbe fecit Jovinianus, ut eum conferret Manichaeo, putaretque nihil interesse inter nuptiarum accusatorem et laudatorem2. Nam si de legitima et a Deo instituta corporum conjunctione generatos, posteaquam usum coeperunt habere rationis. sponte propria proborum ' imitatione mentitos dixit Ambrosius; non tamen hanc conjunctionem, mendacii voluit necessitatem videri, sed universitatis indicium t. Tale est enim quod dixit, Nati ex parentibus mentiuntur; quale si dixisset, Omnis homo, duntaxat sui rector arbitrii, aliquando mentitus est : sciebat quippe neminem sine cominixtione parentum, praeter Christum, exstitisse. Igitur opere conjugali non iniquitatem, sed generalitatem vir prudens voluit indicari. Christum vero pronuntiavit omne cavisse mendacium, quem wiraculo parientis ostendit : quod quidem vehementer contra Hieronymum, cujus tu assecla es, fremit; qui mendacium signalissime Christo est conatus affigere (a). Non ergo jure vocatus est Manichaeus (si tamen vocatus), qui contra errorem vestrum frequentavit laudationem creaturarum.
passages.english: …nor said that the union of spouses was either the work of the devil or a necessity of sin: Jovinian acted wickedly in comparing him to a Manichaean and in thinking there was no difference between the accuser and the praiser of marriage. For if Ambrose said that those born of the lawful bodily union instituted by God, after they began to have the use of reason, lied of their own will in imitation of the wicked, he nevertheless did not want this union to seem the necessity of lying, but an indication of universality. For what he said, "Those born of parents lie," is the same as if he had said, "Every man, at least the ruler of his own choice, has at some time lied": for he knew that no one, except Christ, had come into existence without the union of parents. So the prudent man wished to indicate by the conjugal act not iniquity but generality. But he declared that Christ, whom he showed [born] by a miracle of the one bearing him, avoided all lying: and this indeed rages vehemently against Jerome, whose follower you are, who most notably tried to fasten a lie upon Christ. So he was not rightly called a Manichaean (if indeed he was so called), who, against your error, frequently praised created things.
passages.notes: Julian's words quoted by Augustine. "proborum" likely corrupt for "improborum" ("of the wicked"); translated so. "indicium t" footnote mark omitted; "wiraculo" read as "miraculo".

passages.original: cum hoc faciat secundum fidem nostram ? Quomodo autem illa verba posuerit, quae a me tibi objecta tu commemorare timuisti, ne tenebra tuae clarissima luce illorum redarguerentur , aliis eliam scriptorum suorum locis sic ostendit Ambrosius, ut non ei sicut negligentiori, quomodo loqueris, et incautiori sententia ista semel subrepsisse videatur; sed de peccato originali dogma ejus, quoniam dogma catholicum est, satis liquida manifestatione declaret.
passages.english: …since he does this according to our faith? But how he set down those words, which I cited against you and you were afraid to mention lest your darkness be refuted by their brilliant light, Ambrose shows in other places of his writings too, in such a way that this view does not seem to have slipped from him once, as from a rather careless and incautious man, as you put it; but he declares with quite clear manifestation his doctrine on original sin, since it is catholic doctrine.

passages.original: Cum illo igitur, secundum vos, sumus et Manichæi, et pejores Joviniano, et quidquid nos aliud ore protervo , nec sane veridico, sed maledico dixeritis, docuit nos Dominus gaudere et exsultare, quando qualiacumque maledicta non ex veritate audimus, sed quia pro veritatecertamus (Matth. v, 12). Ecce ego non dicomali esse necessitatem, quia nec Ambrosius; et tamen dico ' parvulos a malitia reformari, quod et Ambrosius : et ideo mali nulla est necessitas; quia et iMud Den sa nabile cst, quod trahit nativitas; quanto magis quod addit voluntas ? Non dico, nec per gratiam Immines liberari; quod absit ut dicat Ambrosius : sed quod non vis dicimus, nonnisi per gratiam liberari , non solum ut eis debita dimittantur, verum etiam ne in tentationem inferantur.
passages.english: With him, then, according to you, we are both Manichaeans and worse than Jovinian, and whatever else you say of us with your impudent mouth, not truthful but slanderous—the Lord has taught us to rejoice and exult when we hear abuse of any kind, not according to the truth, but because we contend for the truth (Matt. 5:12). See, I do not say there is a necessity of evil, because neither does Ambrose; and yet I say that infants are reformed from malice, as Ambrose does too: and therefore there is no necessity of evil, because even that which birth draws along is curable by God; how much more what the will adds? I do not say that people are not freed even through grace—far be it that Ambrose should say this—but we say, what you do not want, that they are freed only through grace, not only so that their debts may be forgiven, but also so that they may not be led into temptation.
passages.notes: "iMud Den sa nabile" read as "illud Deo sanabile".

passages.original: Quid est ergo quod dicis, « Vide itaque quam non de eo loquatur erimine, quod confingit Manichæus ? » ubi vis intelligi originale peccatum; quod non confingit Manichæus, sed, ut caeteri Catholici, et contra vos, et contra Manichæum confitetur Ambrosius : quia non est alienae naturae commixtio, quam Manichæus inducit; sed nostrae depravatio de peccato , quod in mundum per unum hominem intravit, ct per omnes homines pertransiit, quod contra fidem catholicam vos negatis.
passages.english: What then is it that you say: "See, therefore, how he is not speaking of the crime that the Manichaean invents"? By which you want original sin to be understood; which the Manichaean does not invent, but Ambrose, like the other Catholics, confesses against both you and the Manichaean: because it is not a mixture of an alien nature, which the Manichaean introduces, but a depravation of our own [nature] from the sin which entered the world through one man and passed through to all men, which you deny against the catholic faith.

passages.original: Hoc ergo malum, quo caro concupiscit adversus spiritum , hæreticus Julianus dicit esso bonum : hoc malum ex aliena mali natura nobis esse commixtum dicit alus hæreticus Manichæus : hoc malum per prævaricationem primi hominis in nostram dicens vertisse naturam, Catholicus ambos vincit Ambrosius.
passages.english: This evil, then, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, the heretic Julian says is good; this evil the other heretic, the Manichaean, says has been mixed into us from an alien nature of evil; this evil Ambrose the Catholic, saying that it was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man, overcomes them both.

passages.original: Auc. Usus fcminx naturalis est, cam ejus masculus illo membro utitur, quo natura ejusdem generis animantium propagatur : propter quod ctiam ipsun. membrum natura proprie dici solet : unde Cicero ait, mulierem vidisse se in soinnis præsignatam habere naturam ( De Divinatione, lib. 2). Usus itaque naturalis et licitus est, sicut in conjugio ; ct illicitus, i sicut in adulterio : contra naturam vero semper illi- ' citus, et procul dubio flagitiosior atque turpior;
passages.english: AUG. The natural use of a woman is when the male uses that member of hers by which the nature of that kind of living creature is propagated: for which reason that member itself is commonly called properly "nature"; hence Cicero says that a woman saw herself in dreams having her "nature" sealed up (On Divination, book 2). So the natural use is both lawful, as in marriage, and unlawful, as in adultery; but [use] against nature is always unlawful, and without doubt more shameful and base;
passages.notes: "feminae" etc. read for scanning errors.

passages.original: Quod autem me solum affirmas dicere bonas nuptias, reamque naturam : ut alios taceam, do tibi Paulum apostolum, quem tu quoque laudatorem praedicas nuptiarum, dicentem tamen de naturae originalis 1 reatu, corpus mortuum esse propter peccatum (Rom. VIII, 10). Do tibi alterum Injus intellectorem , meumque doctorem, catholicum Ambrosium, qui cum laudet conjugalem pudicitiam, dicit tamen : « Omnes sub peccato nascimur, quorum ipse ortus in vitio est i (De Pænitentia , lib. 1, cap. 2 vel 3). Calumniose, contentiose I, linguose, quid quaeris amplius?
passages.english: As for your claim that I alone say that marriage is good and that nature is guilty: to say nothing of others, I give you the apostle Paul, whom you too proclaim a praiser of marriage, who nevertheless says concerning the guilt of original nature that the body is dead because of sin (Rom. 8:10). I give you another, his interpreter and my teacher, the catholic Ambrose, who, though he praises conjugal chastity, nevertheless says: "We are all born under sin, we whose very origin is in fault" (On Penance, book 1, ch. 2 or 3). Slanderous, contentious, garrulous man, what more do you seek?
passages.notes: "Injus" read as "hujus".

passages.original: quod enim dicit eliam ille, non ila dicimns sicut ille Nos enim naturam nostram bonam voluntario peccato illius ex quo nati sumus, dicimus esse vitiatam, unde omnes sub peccato nascimur, et ipse noster ortus in vitio est, quod dicit Ambrosius ( De Pænitentia, lib. i , cap. i vel 3 ) : ille autem naturam malam nobis porlat1 alienam , cujus nos affirmat commixtione peccare. Denique, nos sanandæ nostrae etiam parvulos offerimus Salvatori : ille autem Christum non idco existimat necessarium , ut naturam nostram sanct in nobis , sed ut alienam sejungat a nobis.
passages.english: For what that man also says, we do not say in the way he says it. For we say that our good nature was vitiated by the voluntary sin of him from whom we were born, so that we are all born under sin, and our very origin is in vice, as Ambrose says (On Repentance, book 1, chapter 1 or 3); but he brings in upon us an evil nature foreign [to us], by whose admixture he asserts that we sin. Finally, we offer even infants to the Saviour so that our [nature] may be healed; but he thinks Christ necessary not in order to heal our nature in us, but to separate a foreign one from us.
passages.notes: "porlat" read as "portat"; "sanct" as "sanet"; "sanandæ nostrae" apparently elliptical for "sanandae nostrae [naturae causa]".

passages.original: et invenies bonum : ea quippe voluntate factus est malus, quæ antequam oriretur ex illo, talis crat, qualis a bono factus erat, id est, bonus. noc est igitur quod ait meus doctor tuusque destructor Ambrosius : Ex bonis igitur mala orta sunt (Lib. de Isaac et Anima, cap. 7). Quod tu negando, et dicendo, Rerum ratio non ,inii, ut de bono malum, et de justo injustum aliquid proferatur; tantum adjuvas Manichxos ad introducendam naturam mali, de qua dicunt oriri mala , ut te patronum sui gratulentur errot is , nisi cum eis et ipse vincaris.
passages.english: and you will find [him] good; for he was made evil by that will which, before it arose from him, was such as he had been made by the Good One, that is, good. This, then, is what my teacher and your destroyer Ambrose says: "So evils arose from good things" (On Isaac and the Soul, chapter 7). By denying this and saying, "The order of things does not allow that evil be brought forth from good, and something unjust from the just," you help the Manichaeans so much in introducing a nature of evil, from which they say evils arise, that they would congratulate you as the patron of their error, were you not yourself defeated along with them.
passages.notes: "non ,inii" read as "non sinit".

passages.original: sani negare non possunt, oriri ab unoquoque voluntatem suam, nec nisi ab homine oriri hominis voluntatem. Ac per boc,quoniam mala hominum mala voluntate esse cœperunt, et ante voluntatem malam scimus fuisse hominum naturam bonam ; ex bonis orta sunt mala. Iloc dicit Ambrosius ; hinc perimitur Manichaeus: hoc pro Manichæo negat contra Ambrosium Julianus, dicens, i Si natura opus Dei est, per opus Dei opus diaboli transire non sinitur ; v ut Manichæus dicat, non esse homines opus Dei, per quos Apostolus transisse dicit peccatum et mortem (Rom. v, 12), quod est opus diaboli : quoniam secundum Julianum, « per opus Dei opus diaboli transire non sinitur; » et dicit Apostolus per homines transisse opus diaboli; non sunt ergo * homines opus Dei.
passages.english: those of sound mind cannot deny that each person's will arises from himself, and that a human's will arises only from a human. And therefore, since human evils began through an evil will, and we know that before the evil will human nature was good, evils arose from good things. This is what Ambrose says; by this the Manichaean is slain; this Julian denies on behalf of the Manichaean against Ambrose, saying, "If nature is the work of God, the work of the devil is not allowed to pass through the work of God"; so that the Manichaean may say that humans are not the work of God, through whom the Apostle says sin and death passed (Rom. 5:12), which is the work of the devil: since according to Julian "the work of the devil is not allowed to pass through the work of God," and the Apostle says the work of the devil passed through humans; therefore humans are not the work of God.

passages.original: Si ergo homo voluit, de homine exstitit : et quid erat homo, antequam de illo existeret, nisi natura bona et bonum opus Dei ? Quod est etiam malus homo, in quantum homo est et opus Dei. Confundatur ergo sua vanitate Julianus; quoniam ex bonis esse mala orta, verum' dixit Ambrosius (De Isaac et Amma, cap. 7): sed quia cogente nullo, inculpatus est Deus: quod vero ea permisit existere, usu eorum justo et bono laudatur insignius.
passages.english: If then a man willed, [the evil will] came forth from the man; and what was the man, before it came forth from him, but a good nature and a good work of God? Which even an evil man is, insofar as he is a man and a work of God. Let Julian then be confounded by his own emptiness; for Ambrose spoke the truth that evils arose from good things (On Isaac and the Soul, chapter 7); but because no one compelled [it], God is blameless; and in that he permitted them to exist, he is the more signally praised for his just and good use of them.

passages.original: per quam fit ut homines jam eliam per fidem conversi ad Deum, jam baptizati, sanctificati, in libertatem vocati, non faciant in exstinguenda vitiosa delectatione quae volunt. Verissimumque illud est, quod per antistitem Ambrosium fides catholica dixit, hoc vitium quo caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, per praevaricationem primi hominis in nostram vertisse naturam (Lib. 7 in Luc. XII, 53). Quo telo inevitabili et insuperabili vcritatis , et Manichaeus obtruncatur , et tu. Ambo quippe in hac re, videto 3 quis vestrum pejus, tamen prorsus erratis : tu propterea , quia con.
passages.english: through which it comes about that people already converted to God through faith, already baptized, sanctified, called into freedom, do not do what they will in extinguishing vicious delight. And most true is what the catholic faith said through the bishop Ambrose, that this vice by which the flesh lusts against the spirit turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man (Book 7 on Luke 12:53). By this inescapable and invincible weapon of truth both the Manichaean is cut down and you. For both of you in this matter—see which of you worse—nevertheless go wholly astray: you because you con-
passages.notes: Passage breaks off mid-word ("con-[tendis]").

passages.original: et ascendens ab eo quod non peccare posset, ad id perveniret ubi peccare non posset. Non quippe in corpore spirituali, sed in animali factus erat, quamvis nisi peccasset, minime morituro. Quia, sicut dicit Apostolus, Non prius quod spirituale eat, sed quod animale; postea, spirituale (I Cor. xv, 40). Unde beatus Ambrosius, in umbra vitæ dicit Adam esse factum, de qua posset cadere, non nocessilale, sed voluntate (Lib. de Paradiso). In qua utique si maneret, acciperet eam vitam, cujus illa umbra erat, quam sancti accepturi sunt, ex qua omnino cadere non poterunt.
passages.english: and, ascending from being able not to sin, he would arrive where he could not sin. For he had been made not in a spiritual body but in an animal one, though one that would not have died had he not sinned. Because, as the Apostle says, "Not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; afterwards the spiritual" (1 Cor. 15:46). Hence blessed Ambrose says that Adam was made in a shadow of life, from which he could fall, not by necessity but by will (On Paradise). If he had remained in it, he would surely have received that life of which it was the shadow, which the saints will receive, from which they will be wholly unable to fall.
passages.notes: Reference given as "xv, 40"; the verse is 1 Cor. 15:46.

passages.original: et sive ut tu, sive uberius atque copiosius, tamen eadem ipsa garrire, quoe tam manifesta sunt, ut etiam Scripturarum divinarum locis plurimis lectitentur , de corruptibilis corporis onere, ct ex illo• animæ aggravatione venientia. Unde et in sanctis, in hujus vitæ agone luctantibus, caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem (Galat. v, 17) : cum spiritus, sicut ait gloriosissimus Cyprianus, cœlestia atque divina quærit, caro terrena et sæcularia concupiscit (De Oratione Dominica). Hinc est ille conflictus, quem memoratus martyr in libro, quem de Mortalitate conscripsit, diligenter et eloquenter explicat, dicens inter caetera, quod nobis sit cum carnalibus vitiis atque illecebris sæcularibus assidua et molesta luctatio.
passages.english: and, whether as you do or more richly and copiously, to chatter those very same things which are so obvious that they are read in very many places of the divine Scriptures, about the burden of the corruptible body and the weighing down of the soul that comes from it. Hence even in the saints, struggling in the contest of this life, the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17): since the spirit, as the most glorious Cyprian says, seeks heavenly and divine things, the flesh lusts for earthly and worldly things (On the Lord's Prayer). Hence that conflict which the said martyr explains carefully and eloquently in the book he wrote On Mortality, saying among other things that we have a constant and troublesome wrestling with carnal vices and worldly allurements.

passages.original: Pax vero, ubi non eas adversantes repugnantesque patiamur, fuit in corpore vitc illius, qnam natura vitiata primi bominis prævaricatione perdidimus. Nam si nec ibi fuit ante peccatum pax carnis ct spiritus, falsumque est quod ait Ambrosius, utriusque discordiam per prævaricationem primi hominis in nostram vertisse naturam (Lib. 7 in Luc. XII, 55) : vera crit, quod absit, ista sententia, quam contra nos Manichæum fecisti loquentem, miserum, scilicet animal primum hominem conditum, quem cupiditas innata reddebat inquietum, quam cupiditatem rei interdictos ei venustas irritabat et suavitas.
passages.english: But peace, where we would not suffer them opposing and resisting, existed in the body of that life which we lost, our nature vitiated by the transgression of the first man. For if even there before sin there was no peace of flesh and spirit, and what Ambrose says is false, that the discord of the two turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man (Book 7 on Luke 12:55), then true—God forbid—will be that opinion which you made the Manichaean speak against us: that the first man was created a wretched animal, whom an innate desire made restless, a desire which the beauty and sweetness of the forbidden thing provoked.

passages.original: cogimusque ut explicet, quid putet esse peccatum, quod claret nihil esse aliud, quam voluntatem appetentem quod justitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Quo constituto, omnes illi oblocutionom rubi, qui concretionem corporum pupugerant, radicitus, et ut ille ait, eradicitus monstrantur evulsi (Cicero, lib. i de Finibus). Jam vero affestus timoris et sensus doloris, per quos in naufragia hominum cieri tempestatem putavit, non solum nullius mali coactores, sed cum 1 repagulum bonae voluntatis nacti sunt, adjutores et pervectores 2 justitiae perdocentur.
passages.english: and we compel him to explain what he thinks sin is, which is clearly nothing other than a will seeking what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain. This established, all those brambles of abuse which had pricked at the composition of bodies are shown to be torn up by the roots and, as that man says, "uprooted" (Cicero, De Finibus book 1). And now the emotion of fear and the sense of pain, through which he thought a storm was stirred up for the shipwreck of humans, are shown not only to be compellers of no evil, but, when they have found the bar of a good will, to be helpers and conveyors of justice.
passages.notes: Julian speaking. "radicitus... eradicitus": a wordplay hard to render.

passages.original: liis ipsam debere naturam, cum quisque cogitaret esse pns,e lilium suum, cujus eam videret anatem, ut ex quucumque femina ignota qua indifferenter usus esset, suo natus semine non immerito crederetur. Quid ? illam vocem noxne de visceribus cunctorum patrum Cicero emisit ad lilium, ad quem scribens ait, « Solus es omnium, a quo me in omnibus vinci velim ? > Nonne ipsa quæ occultissima esse diximus, et tamen plus quam credibile est valere cognoscimus, naturalia propaginis jura fecerunt', ut duo gemini non solum nondum gignentes, verum etiam nondum uascenles, adhuc in utero matris, duo populi dicerentur (Gen.
passages.english: the very nature owes to [their children], since each would think his son to be [one] whose mother he saw, so that from whatever unknown woman he had used indiscriminately, [a child] born of his seed might not undeservedly be believed [his]. What? Did not Cicero utter from the bowels of all fathers that cry to his son, to whom he says in writing, "You alone of all are the one by whom I would wish to be surpassed in everything"? Did not those very natural laws of descent, which we said are most hidden and yet we know have more force than is credible, bring it about that two twins, not only not yet begetting but not yet even born, still in their mother's womb, were called two peoples (Gen. 25:23)?
passages.notes: Opening badly garbled ("liis... pns,e lilium... anatem"); read roughly as "[fi]liis... posse filium... matrem"; first clause uncertain.

passages.original: Nec parvulos non habentes nisi originale peccatum, omnibus flagitiosis et sceleratis, at calumniaris, judico esse pejores. Aliud est enim peccato a se commisso gravari, aliud alieni quamlibet magni contagione respergi. Propter quod parvuli ad remissionem peccatorum, sicut ait Poenus, paena vestra, Cyprianus, hoc ipso facitins accedunt, quod eis remittuntur non propria , sed aliena peccata (Epill. 64, ad Fidum). Tu autem, cum parvulos , non solum, quod et nos dicimus, nullum ex propria voluntate fecisse, verum etiam nullum dicis ex origine traxisse peccatum, injustum procul dubio facis Deum, quod tibi jam saepe dictum, srepiusque dicendum est, qui eis imposuit grave jugum a die exitus de ventre matris illorum.
passages.english: Nor do I judge that little children, who have no sin but original sin, are worse than all the shameful and wicked, as you slanderously claim. For it is one thing to be weighed down by a sin one has committed oneself, another to be spattered by the contagion of another's sin, however great. For this reason little children come to the remission of sins, as the Carthaginian Cyprian, your punishment, says, all the more easily for this very reason, that it is not their own but another's sins that are remitted to them (Epistle 64, to Fidus). But you, since you say that little children have not only committed no sin of their own will, which we also say, but have also contracted no sin from their origin, beyond doubt make God unjust, as has already often been said to you and must be said more often still, [God] who laid a heavy yoke on them from the day of their coming forth from their mother's womb.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'at calumniaris' read as 'ut calumniaris'; 'facitins' as 'facilius'; 'srepiusque' as 'saepiusque'. 'Poenus, paena vestra' is a wordplay (Poenus 'the Carthaginian' / poena 'punishment'), lost in English. The final clause alludes to Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 40:1.
